title: Kalidasa's Birth of Kumara — the Sanskrit text
altTitles: The Birth of the War God
author: kalidasa
attributionNote: The mahākāvya of Kālidāsa on the marriage of Shiva and Pārvatī and the birth of their son, and one of the two poems of his the tradition counted as its models; the eighth sarga was famous enough to be quoted as a test of style. The text as GRETIL publishes it has eight sargas.
description: The Kumārasaṃbhava tells how the Himalaya's daughter was born and grew, how the god of love was burnt when he aimed his arrow at Shiva's meditation, how Pārvatī won the great ascetic by her own penance and was married with the gods as guests, and how Kumāra, the war god who defeats the demon Tāraka, was conceived and born in the reeds of the Ganges. Its descriptions of the Himalaya, of the spring, of the burning of Kāma and of the wedding are the finest nature and love poetry in Sanskrit, and it ends with the child of the destroying god as the protector of the world.
historicalContext: The poem shaped the Shaiva devotional sensibility of the classical and medieval periods — the bridal mysticism of later Indian literature begins in it — and it was translated and imitated from Java to Kashmir; a substantial Tamil, Kannada and Marathi tradition of retelling it attests its popularity beyond Sanskrit.
availabilityNote: Partial as GRETIL publishes it: the eight sargas it gives, 613 verses, streamed from GRETIL at read time, one sarga at a time. Later sargas have been doubted or assigned to other hands and are not part of this transcription, and the work is not claimed as complete. This is the original Sanskrit, not a translation.
